statement: In people who use drugs in North America who tested their drugs (or, in one study, their urine) with fentanyl test strips, themselves at home or with staff at a supervised injection site (2016 to 2023), a result showing fentanyl was followed, by people's own account, by a safer way of using in a minority to a majority of cases, most often using less or going slower, and seldom by throwing the drug away; no study read observed what people then took. In a Rhode Island research pilot (2017), of 31 young adults who said a strip had shown fentanyl, 45 in 100 said they then used smaller amounts, 42 went slower, 39 used with someone else around, 36 tried a small amount first (a 'tester'), 10 threw the drugs out, 10 sold them and 7 gave them away; these answers were given at least two weeks later, the results were not checked, and how many used the drugs as usual was not reported. At a Vancouver supervised injection site (2016 to 2017), staff recorded an intention to use less after 142 of 391 checks before use that showed fentanyl (36 in 100), against 7 of 122 that did not (6 in 100), and an intention to throw the drug away after 50 of 436 (11 in 100) against 10 of 134 (7 in 100); what people then did was not recorded. In a British Columbia take-home programme (2019), asked a standard question (not about their own results) about what they did when a strip showed fentanyl, 217 of 336 answers (65 in 100) described no change, 86 (26 in 100) at least one safer change and 6 (2 in 100) a riskier one (using alone, or using more or faster). Reviews relay a median of 55 in 100 (23 to 75 in 100, seven studies) reporting some safer change, people using as usual because of withdrawal, tolerance, doubt about the result or wanting fentanyl, and evidence that is mostly intentions and self-reports without a comparison group; both reviews include the Rhode Island and Vancouver studies. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: When a strip showed fentanyl, some people said they used less, went slower, used with someone else nearby or tried a small amount first. Few said they threw the drug away, and in one programme about 2 in 3 answers described no change. All of this is what people said or planned: no study watched what they actually did, and there was no group that did not test to compare with.
population: People who use drugs who tested their drugs (or, in one study, urine) with fentanyl test strips in North America: 31 young adults with a self-reported positive result in a Rhode Island pilot (2017); checks before use at a Vancouver supervised injection site (2016–17); 336 survey answers from 218 people in a British Columbia take-home programme (2019); studies relayed by a scoping review (to March 2023) and a systematic review (to October 2019)
exposure: A fentanyl test strip result showing fentanyl (a positive result)
comparator: A result not showing fentanyl (Vancouver checks only); otherwise none
outcome: Self-reported actions after a positive result (at follow-up), intentions recorded by staff right after the result, and answers to standard questions about what people did after a positive result
magnitude: Krieger (31 with a positive result): smaller amounts 45%, went slower 42%, used with someone else 39%, did a tester 36%, threw out 10%, sold 10%, gave away 7%. Karamouzian (checks before use): intended dose reduction 142/391 (36.3%; Wilson 31.7–41.2%) after a positive against 7/122 (5.7%; 2.8–11.4%) after a negative, crude OR 9.36 (4.25–20.65), risk difference 30.6 points (Newcombe 23.3–36.3; editors' calculations); intended disposal 50/436 (11.5%) against 10/134 (7.5%), OR 1.60 (0.79–3.26). Klaire (336 answers to standard questions): no change 217 (64.6%), at least one safer change 86 (25.6%; Wilson 21.2–30.5%), riskier 6 (1.8%; 0.8–3.8%; editors' calculations). Kutscher (relayed): any safer change median 55% (range 23–75%), seven studies, eight locations. Maghsoudi (relayed): 43% of 125 people who inject drugs at a US syringe services programme reported changing behaviour, more often when fentanyl was detected (adjusted OR 5.08, 2.12–12.17).

evidence.extracted: At follow-up, participants who reported a positive result were asked what they did after finding out their drugs had fentanyl. 31 of the 62 who used a strip (50%) reported at least one positive result (not verified). Of these 31, who had tested their drugs or urine, 45% used smaller amounts, 42% went slower, 39% used with someone else around, 36% did a tester, 10% threw their drugs out, 10% sold them and 7% gave them away (more than one answer allowed); 'took them anyways' was an answer option, but how many chose it is not reported. Editors' calculation: 45%, 42%, 39% and 10% fit 14, 13, 12 and 3 of 31; 36% and 7% cannot be formed from 31 (card reporting issue).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph; Table 3, 1st row and footnote
evidence.extracted: The authors note that the answers were self-reported, open to social desirability and recall bias, and that strip results were not verified. Table 3's behaviour-change composite counts 6 of the 19 who used no strip and 4 of the 31 without a positive result, and its footnote includes 'Took them anyways', so the composite is not used here (card reporting issues).

Before use, staff recorded a stated intention to reduce the dose after 142 of 391 fentanyl-positive checks (36.3%) against 7 of 122 negative checks (5.7%), crude OR 9.36 (95% CI 4.25–20.65), and an intention to dispose of the drug after 50 of 436 positive checks (11.5%) against 10 of 134 negative checks (7.5%), OR 1.60 (0.79–3.26). Intentions were stated to staff after the result and what people then did was not recorded; intentions were not reported for checks made after use. Editors' calculation (card): risk difference for dose reduction 30.6 percentage points (Newcombe 95% CI 23.3–36.3).

evidence.locator: Methods › Survey tools and testing kits, 2nd paragraph (p. 3); Results, 8th paragraph (p. 4)
evidence.extracted: On returning a results sheet, participants answered standard questions, not based on their own returned results, about what they did after a positive or a negative result. For a positive result, 217 (64.6%) reported no behaviour change and 86 (25.6%) at least one safer change: using less or more slowly 45, using with someone else 26, using at an overdose prevention or supervised consumption site 9, not using at all 7, having someone check on them 4; 6 (1.8%) reported a riskier change (1 using more or more quickly, 5 using alone). The denominator is 336 survey answers from 218 people, so people who returned several sheets count more than once. Editors' calculation: 86 of 336 is 25.6% (Wilson 95% CI 21.2–30.5%).

evidence.locator: Results › Behavior Change from FTS Results, 1st, 4th and 5th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: As relayed (studies not appraised): across seven studies that did not introduce strips as an intervention, a median of 55% (range 23–75%) of participants in eight locations reported any positive behaviour change; the commonest were using smaller amounts, not using the drug, going slower and using a tester shot, with actual and hypothetical reports counted together in Table 4. People may use drugs as usual despite a positive result because of withdrawal, existing harm-reduction practice, tolerance or indifference to fentanyl, doubt about the result, or wanting fentanyl. People who use drugs often use harm-reduction tools whether or not they use strips.

evidence.locator: Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Results › Study quality
evidence.extracted: Systematic review of drug checking services to October 2019: of 31 studies on behaviour, 22 measured intentions (in response to actual or hypothetical results) and 16 enacted behaviour, observed by staff or self-reported from recall. 43% of 125 people who inject drugs at a US syringe services programme (2017) reported changing behaviour, more often when fentanyl was detected (adjusted OR 5.08, 95% CI 2.12–12.17; primary study not read). The 13 appraised articles scored 3 to 7 of 14 points (cross-sectional studies), and the authors judged all of relatively poor quality. The review includes the Rhode Island pilot (n = 81) and the Vancouver study.

risk_of_bias.note: Self-reports and intentions given to research or service staff (social desirability), unverified strip results (Rhode Island), intentions not followed up (Vancouver), people who chose to test; the take-home answers are standard questions not tied to people's own results (ROBINS-I critical for Krieger et al. and Karamouzian et al., serious for Klaire et al.).

inconsistency.note: The shares differ (26 to 75 in 100 reporting some safer change), largely in line with how the question was asked (what people did, what they intended, a standard question) and the setting; the pattern (using less or slower most often, throwing away seldom) is the same.

indirectness.note: Intentions and standard-question answers stand in for what people did; all North American settings where fentanyl was common; responses to a negative result are not reported.

imprecision.note: The Rhode Island percentages rest on 31 people, but the other studies are larger.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive claim; observational, starts low; risk of bias and indirectness each take a level: very low. Rated as worded: what people said they did or intended after a positive result, not whether testing changed behaviour. The Rhode Island behaviour-change composite (21 of 31 against 4 of 31) is not used, because it was assigned to people with no positive result and its comparison is confounded (card sc_krieger_2018, reporting issues). Counted once: Krieger et al. and Karamouzian et al. are inside both reviews. Status replicated: independent studies in Rhode Island, at a Vancouver supervised injection site and in a British Columbia take-home programme point the same way.
